The text says Herodotus described the Hawara Labyrinth as the greatest architectural achievement in all history and the single greatest wonder of the ancient world.
Herodotus said the labyrinth was superior to the Giza Pyramids, which he said were superior to all the works of the Greeks.
Herodotus wrote that the labyrinth had twelve covered courts with gates facing one another, six on the north side and six on the south side.
Herodotus wrote that the labyrinth had two kinds of chambers, one below ground and one above, with 3,000 chambers in total and 1,500 of each kind.

Herodotus wrote that the upper chambers were seen directly by him and his companions, while the underground chambers were only heard about because the Egyptians who had charge of them would not show them.
Herodotus wrote that the passages through the chambers and courts were admiringly adorned and created endless marvels.
Herodotus wrote that the whole structure had a stone roof, walls covered with carved figures, and courts surrounded by perfectly fitted white stone pillars.
Herodotus wrote that at the end of the labyrinth, by one corner, there was a pyramid of forty fathoms with large figures carved on it and an underground way leading to it.
Diodorus Siculus wrote that a native king named Mendes, whom some call Mares, built the Labyrinth as a tomb.
Diodorus Siculus said the Labyrinth was wonderful not so much for its size as for the inimitable skill with which it was built.
Diodorus Siculus wrote that it was impossible to find one’s way out of the Labyrinth without difficulty unless one had a guide perfectly acquainted with it.
Diodorus Siculus said the Egyptian Labyrinth remained absolutely perfect in its entire construction down to his time.
Diodorus Siculus wrote that the builders chose a site beside the channel leading into Lake Moeris in Libya.
Diodorus Siculus wrote that the tomb was constructed of the finest stone in an oblong shape with each side measuring a stade.
Diodorus Siculus wrote that the sacred enclosure contained a temple surrounded by columns, forty to each side.
Diodorus Siculus wrote that the building had a roof made of a single stone carved with panels and richly adorned with excellent paintings.
Diodorus Siculus wrote that it contained memorials of the homeland of each king and of the temples and sacrifices carried out there.
Diodorus Siculus wrote that the kings conceived their tomb on such an expensive and prodigious scale that their successors could not surpass them if the tombs had been completed.
Strabo wrote that the total number of nomes was equal to the number of courts in the Labyrinth and that these were fewer than thirty.
Strabo wrote that the Labyrinth was quite equal to the Pyramids and near the tomb of the king who built it.
Strabo wrote of a flat trapezium-shaped site at the channel entrance containing both a village and a great palace made up of many palaces equal in number to the nomes in former times.
Strabo wrote that the palace had many contiguous peristyle courts in one row backing on one wall.
Strabo wrote that hidden chambers were long and many in number, with paths twisting through one another so that no one could enter or leave any court without a guide.
Strabo said the total number of nomes was equal to the number of courts in the Labyrinth and that these were fewer than 30.

Strabo described a flat trapezium-shaped site about 30 or 40 stades from the canal entrance that contained both a village and a great palace made of many palaces equal in number to the nomes in former times.
Strabo said the roofs of the chambers were made of single stones and the widths of the hidden chambers were spanned by monolithic beams, with no wood or other material used.
Strabo said the building had only one storey and that the courts each stood in rows supported by 27 monolithic pillars.
Strabo said the tomb at the end of the building was a pyramid on an oblong base with each side about 4 plethra long and about the same height.
Strabo said the man buried there was named Imandes.
Strabo said the many courts existed because all nomes gathered there by rank with their own priests and priestesses for sacrifice, divine offering, and judgement on the most important matters.
Strabo said each nome was lodged in the court appointed to it.
Strabo said Abydos stood above this city and contained the Memnonium, a palace made of massive stonework like the Labyrinth but simpler in structure.
Pliny the Elder said the Egyptian labyrinth in the Heracleopolite Nome was still standing in his time and was built first, according to tradition, 3,600 years earlier by king Petesuchis or Tithois.
Pliny the Elder said Herodotus ascribed the whole work to Twelve Kings and Psammetichus, the latest of them.
Pliny the Elder said most writers took the Labyrinth to have been built as a temple to the Sun, and he said this view was generally accepted.
Pliny the Elder said Daedalus used the Egyptian Labyrinth as the model for the Labyrinth he built in Crete.
Pliny the Elder said the Egyptian Labyrinth’s twisting paths and passages advanced and retreated and were impossible to negotiate.
Pliny the Elder said the Egyptian specimen had its entrance and columns made of Parian marble and the rest of Aswan granite.
Pliny the Elder said the building was divided into regions and administrative districts called nomes, with each of the 21 nomes giving its name to one of the houses.
Pliny the Elder said the Labyrinth contained temples of all the gods of Egypt and 40 chapels with pyramids of 40 ells each covering an area of 6 arourae at the base.
Pliny the Elder said the maze exhausted travelers, had lofty upper rooms reached by ramps and porticoes, and had stairways with 90 steps each.
Pliny the Elder said the Labyrinth contained columns of imperial porphyry, images of the gods, statues of kings, and representations of monsters.
Pliny the Elder said some halls produced a fearful noise of thunder when the door was opened and that most halls were passed through in darkness.
Pliny the Elder said there were massive buildings outside the wall called “the Wing” and other subterranean chambers made by excavating galleries in the soil.
Pliny the Elder said only one person had repaired the Labyrinth, Chaermon the eunuch of king Necthebis, 500 years before Alexander the Great.
Pliny the Elder said a tradition reported that Chaermon supported the roofs with beams of acacia wood boiled in oil until squared stones could be raised into the vaults.
Pomponius Mela wrote that the Labyrinth of Psammetich included within one unbroken wall 1,000 houses and 12 palaces.
Pomponius Mela wrote that the Labyrinth was built of marble and roofed with the same material.
Pomponius Mela wrote that the Labyrinth had one descending way into it and almost innumerable paths with many convolutions twisting hither and thither.
Pomponius Mela wrote that the paths caused great perplexity because their porticoes often reversed direction and continually ran through one circle after another.
Pomponius Mela wrote that the Labyrinth confused visitors by perpetual meandering, though escape was possible.

Archaeological finds show that the site was continuously occupied up to the 7th century CE.

Flinders Petrie carried out the first large-scale excavations at Hawara in 1888-1889 and 1910-1911.
Petrie found human occupation and activity at Hawara dating from the Middle Kingdom to Coptic times.
Petrie’s most famous finds at Hawara included gilded masks and mummy portraits from late-Ptolemaic and Roman tombs.
Petrie found the wooden panel of Hermione the schoolteacher, one of the very few surviving painted portraits from Classical Antiquity.
In 1888 Petrie focused on the pyramid and the labyrinth and divided the necropolis north of the pyramid into chronological zones from the Middle Kingdom to Byzantine times.
In 1889 Petrie identified the pyramid as that of the 12th dynasty pharaoh Amenemhat III and his daughter Neferuptah.
Petrie cleared a Byzantine basilica northwest of the pyramid.
Petrie identified the actual site of the Egyptian labyrinth in 1888 and said its original foundations allowed its size and orientation to be roughly determined.
Petrie estimated the Labyrinth to be about 304 meters long and 244 meters wide.
Petrie said the structure was large enough to hold the great temples of Karnak and Luxor.
Petrie concluded that the brick chambers Lepsius thought belonged to the Labyrinth were remains of the Roman town built by its supposed destroyers.
Petrie concluded that the Labyrinth had been so thoroughly demolished that only a great bed of fragments remained on top of an artificial stone foundation.

Petrie found scattered bits of foundations, a great well, two door jambs, two granite shrines and part of another, several fragments of statues, and a large granite seated figure of the king at Hawara.
Petrie identified the king as Amenemhet III of the XIIth Dynasty, also known as Lampares, who reigned in the 23rd century BCE.
In 1911 Petrie returned to Hawara to excavate in the labyrinth and to find more Faiyum portraits on Roman-period mummies.
Petrie’s 1911 reconstructions were still mainly based on classical authors and only partly on the evidence he found.
Petrie wrote that the brick chambers on the site were village houses built on top of the ruins of a great stone structure.
Petrie wrote that beneath the brick chambers lay layers of stone chips over a vast area and a uniform smooth bed of beton or plaster under the fragments.
Petrie said the chip stratum was about six feet thick and ended abruptly at the limit of the building where the canal had cut across the site.
Petrie said no trace of architectural arrangement could be found to identify the great structure with the labyrinth, but its extent showed it was far larger than any temple known in Egypt.
Petrie said the temples of Karnak, Luxor, and several on the west side of Thebes could all fit inside the vast space of the Hawara buildings.
Petrie said the labyrinth had long been a quarry for the district and that its destruction occupied such a body of masons that a small town existed there.
Petrie said the recorded position of the site matched what could be traced and that no doubt could remain regarding the position of one of the wonders of Egypt.
